content: Studies conducted in England have indicated that individuals with higher socioeconomic status are more likely to accept antihypertensive drug therapy. In one study, 35% of Caucasians and 20% of South Asians in the two lowest socioeconomic categories reported that they would not accept antihypertensive drug therapy. Shahaj et al. synthesized six qualitative and 29 quantitative reviews, identifying various individual and social factors that influence treatment adherence. These factors include familial issues (such as lack of support or the need for separate meals) and environmental factors (such as a sense of security, availability of local amenities, and access to healthy food). A review by Fragasso et al. highlighted that quality of life during antihypertensive therapy is a significant concern, as clinicians often initiate treatment in asymptomatic patients who may experience side effects that make them symptomatic. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) acknowledged variability in stakeholder values but concluded that initiating hypertension (HTN) medications is generally feasible and acceptable. Regarding costs, thiazide-like diuretics, ACE inhibitors (ACEis), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and long-acting dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs) are available as generic drugs, are simple to manufacture, and should be globally accessible at low cost. Other costs, such as workforce requirements, infrastructure, laboratory testing, and lost work time, are real but modest. Numerous modeling studies have demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of antihypertensive therapy, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where many adults have untreated hypertension, provided medications are available at low cost. Models from countries such as Bangladesh, Ghana, and Nigeria support this conclusion. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends combination therapy, preferably in a single-pill form, as an initial treatment for adults with hypertension requiring pharmacological intervention. This approach improves adherence and persistence. The combination therapy should include drugs from three classes: diuretics (thiazide or thiazide-like), ACEis/ARBs, and long-acting dihydropyridine CCBs. Single-pill combinations are particularly valuable when baseline BP is ≥20/10 mmHg above the target. Evidence suggests that single-pill combinations improve medication adherence and BP control compared to multiple-pill regimens. The GDG reviewed evidence comparing monotherapy and combination therapy as first-line treatments for hypertension. While data on mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were imprecise, combination therapy was associated with fewer side effects due to the use of lower doses of each drug. A large non-randomized study in Italy found that initiating treatment with a two-drug single-pill or free combination significantly reduced the risk of death (by 20%) and hospitalization for cardiovascular events (by 16%) compared to monotherapy. Combination therapy also improves adherence and persistence, with single-pill combinations showing an 8–14% higher medication possession ratio and twice the likelihood of persistence compared to free-equivalent components. The rationale for recommending combination therapy, particularly in a single-pill form, is based on several factors: most individuals with hypertension will eventually require two or more agents to achieve BP control; combining two agents from complementary classes provides greater BP reduction efficacy; lower doses of each agent reduce side effects; adherence and persistence are improved; and simplified logistics reduce stock-outs and pharmacy inventory issues. However, challenges such as limited flexibility in dose adjustments and difficulty attributing side effects to specific components remain. WHO recommends a target BP of <140/90 mmHg for all patients with hypertension without comorbidities and <130 mmHg for those with known cardiovascular disease (CVD) or high-risk conditions such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Evidence from systematic reviews and trials like SPRINT suggests that lower BP targets reduce mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and stroke risk, though they may increase the risk of serious adverse events. The GDG emphasized caution in applying this evidence to lower-risk patients and noted that the benefits of intensive treatment must be balanced against potential harms, particularly in older adults. For follow-up, WHO suggests monthly visits after initiating or changing antihypertensive medications until the target BP is achieved. Once BP is controlled, follow-up every 3–6 months is recommended. Evidence from trials and systematic reviews supports shorter follow-up intervals for better BP control and monitoring of side effects, though longer intervals may lead to loss to follow-up. The GDG acknowledged the burden of frequent follow-ups on patients and health systems but emphasized their potential benefits in improving adherence and outcomes. WHO also supports the involvement of non-physician professionals, such as pharmacists and nurses, in managing hypertension, provided they receive proper training, have prescribing authority, follow specific management protocols, and operate under physician oversight. Community health workers can assist with education, medication delivery, and BP monitoring as part of a collaborative care model. Evidence suggests that non-physician management is not inferior to physician management and can improve BP control, though data on cardiovascular events and harms are limited.
